stories.title: Count with the Frog
stories.name: Katherine Johnson
stories.who: NASA mathematician who loved to count
stories.story: Katherine Johnson grew up in West Virginia, in the USA. She said that she counted everything. She counted the steps to the road and the steps up to church. She counted the dishes she washed, too. She kept loving numbers and grew up to work at NASA. In 1961 her sums helped plan the path of a spaceflight for an astronaut called Alan Shepard.
stories.link_to_lesson: Katherine loved counting steps and spotting numbers, and today we count in jumps of 2s, 3s and 5s to find patterns.

try_it.q: Katherine counted steps. Count in 5s: 5, 10, 15, __, __. What are the next two numbers?

stories.icon: A pair of footprints climbing three steps, each step with a number on it.

stories.title: Number Bond Inquiry
stories.name: Carl Friedrich Gauss
stories.who: German mathematician famous for clever number tricks
stories.story: A story often told about young Gauss goes like this. His teacher asked the class to add 1 + 2 + 3 and so on up to 100. Gauss paired the numbers: 1 and 100 make 101, 2 and 99 make 101, and so on. There are 50 pairs, so the answer is 50 times 101, which is 5050. Historians are not sure it happened exactly like this. But pairing numbers is a clever trick you can use too.
stories.link_to_lesson: Gauss's trick uses number bonds: it works by pairing numbers that add up to the same total.

try_it.q: Add 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 using pairs. Which pairs make 7? What is the total?
try_it.a: 1+6, 2+5 and 3+4 each make 7. Three sevens make 21.

stories.legend_note: Legend label used: 'A story often told about young Gauss ... Historians are not sure it happened exactly like this.' The 1-to-100 detail first appears in print long after his childhood.
stories.icon: Two hands joining number tiles that fit together like puzzle pieces, with a star above.

stories.title: Let's Plan the Fruit Party
stories.name: Florence Nightingale
stories.who: Nurse who used coloured charts to show numbers
stories.story: Florence Nightingale is best known as a nurse. She was also very good at statistics, which means collecting and sorting numbers. She turned her numbers into coloured pictures called charts, where a bigger wedge shows a bigger number. A chart helps people see the facts quickly. She used her numbers to show why hospitals needed to be cleaner.
stories.link_to_lesson: Florence turned numbers into pictures so that people could read them at a glance, just like a picture graph.

try_it.q: A picture graph shows 4 apples, 2 pears and 5 bananas. Which fruit has the most? How many more bananas than pears?

stories.icon: A lamp with a small round chart made of coloured wedges.

stories.title: Pattern Inquiry
stories.name: Fibonacci (Leonardo of Pisa)
stories.who: Italian maths writer whose growing number pattern has his name
stories.story: Fibonacci lived in Pisa, in Italy, about 800 years ago. As a boy he travelled with his father, who was a merchant. He learned the number signs we use today, 0 to 9. In 1202 he wrote a big book to teach them in Europe. It has a puzzle about rabbits whose answers grow like this: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. People named this pattern after him much later.
stories.link_to_lesson: Fibonacci numbers are a famous growing pattern, and children find the rule that makes it grow.

try_it.q: Fibonacci pattern: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, __, __. Each number is the two before it added together. What comes next?

stories.icon: A spiral of growing squares made of numbered tiles, with a small rabbit.

stories.title: Mystery Number
stories.name: Al-Khwarizmi
stories.country_or_region: Baghdad, now Iraq (his family may have come from Khwarizm in Central Asia)
stories.who: Scholar in Baghdad whose book gave us the word algebra
stories.story: Al-Khwarizmi worked in Baghdad, in a place called the House of Wisdom, about 1,200 years ago. He wrote a book about finding an unknown number. One idea in it is balancing: when you do the same thing to both sides, the two sides stay equal. This helps you undo steps to find the hidden number. His book's title gave us the word algebra. We are not sure where he was born.
stories.link_to_lesson: Finding a mystery number by undoing the steps is the idea behind his book on solving for an unknown number.

try_it.q: I think of a number and add 6. The answer is 14. Work backwards: what is my number?

stories.icon: A balance scale with a question-mark box on one pan.

stories.title: Coin Combos
stories.name: Isaac Newton
stories.who: Famous scientist who also had a job looking after the country's coins
stories.story: Isaac Newton is famous for his big ideas in science. But for many years he also had a job at the Royal Mint, which is where English coins were made. He started there in 1696, when old silver coins were being worn out and replaced with new ones. The people at the Mint cared about every coin having the right weight and the right amount of metal. Newton worked there until 1727.
stories.link_to_lesson: Coins only work as money when each one is made to the right size and weight, so people can count and trade fairly.

try_it.q: You have one 10-cent coin and some 5-cent coins. You want 20 cents. How many 5-cent coins do you need?

stories.icon: A stack of plain round coins next to a small weighing scale.

stories.title: Shape Safari
stories.name: Maryam Mirzakhani
stories.who: Mathematician who thought by drawing shapes and curves
stories.story: Maryam Mirzakhani was born in Tehran, in Iran. As a child she wanted to be a writer. Later she turned to maths, especially geometry, which is the maths of shapes. When she worked on a problem, she drew doodles on big sheets of paper and wrote ideas around the edges. Her daughter called it painting. In 2014 she became the first woman to win the Fields Medal, a top maths prize.
stories.link_to_lesson: Maryam solved problems about shapes by drawing them, and today the children look closely at 2D shapes.

try_it.q: Draw a triangle. How many sides does it have? How many corners?

stories.icon: A big sheet of paper covered in loops, triangles and circles drawn with a pencil.

stories.title: Logic Lab
stories.name: Leonhard Euler
stories.who: Swiss mathematician who drew circles to show groups
stories.story: Leonhard Euler came from Switzerland. Starting in 1760 he wrote letters to a princess in Germany to explain science and ideas to her. In some letters he drew circles to show groups. A small circle inside a big circle shows a smaller group inside a bigger one. Many years later, people called these Euler's circles. Drawing groups as circles still helps us sort things and think clearly.
stories.link_to_lesson: Euler used circles to show how things sort into groups, which is what the children do in Logic and Sorting.

try_it.q: Draw a big circle for animals and a small circle inside it for cats. Is every cat an animal? Is every animal a cat?
try_it.a: Yes, every cat is an animal. No, not every animal is a cat (a dog is an animal but not a cat).

stories.legend_note: Cats-and-animals is our own example, not from Euler's letters.
stories.icon: Two overlapping circles, a small one tucked inside a big one, with a few dots sorted inside.

stories.title: Measure It!
stories.name: Eratosthenes
stories.country_or_region: Ancient Greek world (born in Cyrene, now Libya; worked in Alexandria, Egypt)
stories.who: Head of a great library who measured the whole Earth
stories.story: Eratosthenes was born in Cyrene, which is in Libya today. He worked at the great library in Alexandria, in Egypt, over 2,000 years ago. At noon in midsummer, the Sun was straight overhead in Aswan, far to the south. In Alexandria it was a little to one side. He compared the shadows and used the distance between the two cities. This let him work out how big the Earth is. His answer was quite close.
stories.link_to_lesson: He used the length between two cities, and the lengths of shadows, to measure something huge, just as the children measure lengths today.

try_it.q: One strip is 3 cubes long. Another strip is 5 cubes long. How much longer is the second strip?

stories.icon: A tall stick with a short shadow beside it, and a measuring ruler.

stories.title: Challenge Day
stories.name: Srinivasa Ramanujan
stories.who: Indian mathematician who found surprising patterns in numbers
stories.story: Srinivasa Ramanujan was born in Erode, in India. He loved numbers and worked on maths from a young age. He wrote down his ideas and sent them in letters to mathematicians in England. One of them was G. H. Hardy. Later Ramanujan went to Cambridge to work with him. A story that Hardy told himself: he rode in taxi number 1729 and called it a dull number. Ramanujan said it was very interesting. Even a plain number can hide a surprise.
stories.link_to_lesson: Ramanujan treated numbers like puzzles to explore, which is what the children do on challenge day.

try_it.q: Puzzle: find two numbers that add up to 12 and have a difference of 2.

stories.legend_note: Taxi story labelled as 'a story that Hardy told himself'; it is Hardy's own account of the conversation.
stories.icon: A taxi-shaped number plate showing 1729 with a small lightbulb.
